summary: Updates RFC 7296 so IKEv2 can use raw public keys of types other than RSA, such as elliptic curve keys. This is useful in constrained environments.

eli5.summary: Before, only one kind of ID card was accepted. Now more kinds are, including smaller ones that suit tiny devices.

questions: does ikev2 support raw public keys
how to use elliptic curve raw public keys in ikev2
what is cert encoding 15 in ikev2
subtitle: Lets IKEv2 carry any kind of raw public key, not just RSA, by sending a SubjectPublicKeyInfo structure.

tldr.problem: IKEv2 once supported only RSA raw public keys, and in constrained environments other key types, such as elliptic curve keys, are useful.
tldr.mechanism: A new Certificate Encoding value, 15 (Raw Public Key), carries a PKIX SubjectPublicKeyInfo structure in the Certificate payload, so any key type PKIX defines can be sent.
tldr.outcome: IKEv2 can authenticate peers with any raw public key format, and future key types need no further IKEv2 changes. The RFC updates RFC 7296.

today: RFC 7670 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 7296, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: From RSA-Only to Any Raw Key
sections.content:
This document replaces an algorithm-specific version of raw public keys in the Internet Key Exchange Version 2 (IKEv2) with a generic one. In RFC 5996, IKEv2 supported PKCS #1 encoded RSA keys, a DER-encoded RSAPublicKey structure. Other raw public key types were not supported. RFC 7296 removed even that, and this RFC brings raw public keys back in a more generic way.

The motivation is constrained environments, where other types of public keys, such as those based on Elliptic Curve Cryptography, are useful. The approach mirrors RFC 7250, which does the same for TLS by reusing the SubjectPublicKeyInfo format from the X.509 profile. It supports all public-key formats defined by PKIX and lets future key types work without more IKEv2 changes.
sections.eli5: IKEv2 used to accept just one shape of key, like a lock that only fits one kind of key. Now the lock accepts many shapes, even small ones.

sections.title: The Certificate Payload with a Raw Key
sections.content:
The Certificate payload from RFC 7296 is unchanged in layout: a Next Payload byte, a critical bit, reserved bits, a Payload Length, a one-octet Cert Encoding field and variable-length Certificate Data. This RFC adds one value for Cert Encoding: 15, Raw Public Key.

For that encoding, the Certificate Data is the SubjectPublicKeyInfo structure of a PKIX certificate. It is a simple encoding, because most of the ASN.1 part can be included literally and recognized by block comparison, and it tells the receiver the key type.

The Raw Public Key encoding can also appear in a Certificate Request payload. In that case the Certification Authority field MUST be empty. For RSA keys, implementations MUST follow the public-key processing rules of Section 1.2 of RFC 4055 even though the structure is not part of a certificate, so RSASSA-PSS and RSASSA-PSS-params MUST be sent when applicable.
sections.eli5: The envelope stays the same. There is just a new label on it that says 'this contains a bare public key', and inside is a small standard card describing the key.

sections.title: Signatures and Identity
sections.content:
The base IKEv2 specification supports RSA and DSA signatures. RFC 7427 extended IKEv2 so signature methods over any key type can be used, and implementations using raw public keys SHOULD use the Digital Signature method it describes.

With raw public keys, the identity of the other end is usually the public key itself, not the identity in the ID payload. The ID payload contents might therefore not be useful for authentication, though they can still help with policy decisions such as simplifying a policy lookup. Alternatively, the ID_NULL type from RFC 7619 can be used to show that the ID payload is not relevant to this authentication.
sections.eli5: With a bare key, the key is who you are. The name tag you wear does not prove anything, so it can be left blank.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
A deployment using raw public keys needs an out-of-band public-key validation procedure to be confident the keys are authentic. One way is a configuration mechanism that provisions raw public keys into the IKEv2 software, and the RFC says 'smart object' deployments are likely to use such preconfigured keys. Another is secure DNS, associating keys with domain names using the IPSECKEY DNS RRtype (RFC 4025).

The document does not change the security assumptions of IKEv2, since 'Raw RSA Key' support was already available in RFC 5996. It only generalizes raw public-key support.
sections.eli5: A bare key has no signed ID card from an authority, so you must check some other way that it belongs to the right person, like being handed the key in person.

sections.title: IANA Registration
sections.content: The document allocates one new value in the IKEv2 Certificate Encodings registry: 15, Raw Public Key. Nothing else is registered.
sections.eli5: One new number was added to the official list, so everyone uses the same number for this new kind of key.

sections.title: Worked Examples
sections.content:
The appendix shows complete payloads on the wire. The first uses the 256-bit ECDSA key pair from RFC 4754: algorithm id-ecPublicKey on the fixed curve secp256r1. The bit string in its SubjectPublicKeyInfo is 66 bytes. A first byte of 00 means no unused bits, and the second byte, 04, means uncompressed form, followed by the X and Y values.

The second example uses a random 1024-bit RSA key with algorithm rsaEncryption and exponent 65537. Both end in an IKEv2 Certificate payload where NN stands for the type of the payload that follows.
sections.eli5: The appendix shows two real filled-in envelopes, one with a small modern key and one with an older RSA key, so implementers can check their work.
